Unit 3: Period 3 (1754–1800)

📋 Everything from Unit 3 in one place — the biggest unit, so scan quickly by bolded term. Use the animation to lock in checks and balances before your test.
3.1

Contextualizing Period 3

  • Opens with the Seven Years' War (1754), triggering the chain of events leading to independence.
  • Britain's reassertion of control led to a movement for self-government and the Revolutionary War.
  • After independence, Americans produced the Constitution (1787–88).
  • Period closes around 1800 with the nation's first peaceful transfer of power.
Period 3 at a glance.
3.2

The Seven Years' War

  • British & French colonists competed over the Ohio River Valley.
  • Treaty of Paris (1763): France cedes N. American territory to Britain.
  • Massive British war debt → new taxes on the colonies.
Treaty of Paris 1763Proclamation of 1763
Rivalry to war debt.
3.3

Taxation Without Representation

  • Stamp Act (1765) → Townshend Acts (1767) → Boston Massacre (1770) → Boston Tea Party (1773) → Intolerable Acts (1774).
  • Colonial argument: no representation in Parliament means no legitimate taxation.
  • Sons of Liberty organized resistance through boycotts.
Stamp ActSons of LibertyIntolerable Acts
Trap: The Intolerable Acts backfired — they united the colonies instead of isolating Massachusetts.
Escalating British policy.
3.4

Philosophical Foundations

  • Locke: natural rights (life, liberty, property).
  • Social contract: government power comes from consent of the governed.
  • Declaration of Independence (1776) echoes Locke: unalienable rights.
Natural rightsSocial contractCommon Sense
Ideas → revolutionary argument.
3.5

The American Revolution

  • Lexington & Concord (1775) → Declaration (1776) → Saratoga (1777, turning point, brings French alliance) → Yorktown (1781) → Treaty of Paris (1783).
  • Patriot success: militia resilience, Washington's leadership, French assistance.
Battle of SaratogaBattle of Yorktown
Key turning points.
3.6

Influence of Revolutionary Ideals

  • Northern states begin abolishing slavery; Republican Motherhood reshapes women's civic role.
  • Religious disestablishment spreads in some states.
  • Limits: ideals excluded enslaved people, women's political rights, most Native Americans.
Republican MotherhoodDisestablishment
Ripple effects of the Declaration.
3.7

The Articles of Confederation

  • Deliberately weak central government — no power to tax, no power to regulate trade.
  • Success: Northwest Ordinance (1787).
  • Shays' Rebellion (1786–87) exposed the government's weakness → calls for a stronger constitution.
Articles of ConfederationShays' Rebellion
Rise and failure of the Articles.
3.8

Constitutional Convention & Ratification

  • Great Compromise: two-house Congress (Virginia Plan + New Jersey Plan).
  • Three-Fifths Compromise: enslaved people counted as 3/5 for representation.
  • Federalists (support) vs. Anti-Federalists (opposed, demanded a Bill of Rights).
Great CompromiseThree-Fifths Compromise
Key compromises.
3.9

The Constitution

  • Three branches: legislative (makes laws), executive (enforces), judicial (interprets).
  • Checks and balances: each branch limits the others.
  • Federalism: power divided between national government and states.
Checks and balancesFederalism
Separation of powers.

3.10

Shaping a New Republic

  • Washington forms the first Cabinet; Hamilton's financial plan (national bank) sparks party divisions.
  • Whiskey Rebellion (1794): Washington enforces federal tax authority.
  • Farewell Address (1796): warns against factions & foreign alliances.
Hamilton's financial planWhiskey Rebellion
Precedents, 1789–1798.
3.11

Developing an American Identity

  • Noah Webster's dictionary standardizes American English.
  • Political parties (Federalists vs. Democratic-Republicans) reveal contested visions.
  • Significant regional differences persist between North, South, and West.
Noah WebsterDemocratic-Republicans
Forces shaping identity.
3.12

Movement in the Early Republic

  • Settlers migrate into the Northwest Territory.
  • Northwest Ordinance (1787) organizes territory, bans slavery there.
  • Migration intensifies conflict with Native nations over land.
Northwest Territory
Westward movement.
3.13

Continuity and Change in Period 3

  • Continuity: slavery persists & expands; conflict with Native nations continues.
  • Change: colonies become a unified republic with a written Constitution and new national institutions.
Continuity and change
Continuity vs. change.

Master Summary Table

Compromise / PlanWhat It Resolved
Virginia PlanRepresentation by population (favored large states)
New Jersey PlanEqual representation per state (favored small states)
Great CompromiseTwo-house Congress: House (population) + Senate (equal)
Three-Fifths CompromiseEnslaved people counted as 3/5 for representation & taxation
⚠

Commonly Missed on the Exam

  • Order matters: Saratoga (turning point, French alliance) is not the same as Yorktown (final victory).
  • Anti-Federalists opposed ratification and demanded the Bill of Rights — Federalists supported the Constitution as written.
  • Shays' Rebellion exposed the Articles' weakness, directly leading to the Constitutional Convention.
  • Checks and balances (between branches) vs. federalism (between national/state) are different concepts — don't conflate them.
  • The Whiskey Rebellion tested federal tax authority, distinct from Shays' Rebellion under the Articles.
  • Revolutionary ideals of equality had real limits: did not extend to enslaved people, women's suffrage, or most Native Americans.
